title: Capillary wicking: roll-embossed two-phase cooling film laminated onto memory stacks
idea: Hot-emboss micro-pillar wicks and vapor channels into copper-clad polymer film on R2R lines, then seal and laminate it as an ultra-thin vapor chamber over HBM; capillary pumping returns condensate with no pump.
why: Thermal height limit and refresh (facts 3, 6): 10-20 C lower hot spots allow taller stacks; replaces machined vapor chambers at a fraction of cost.

title: Secondary-market DDR4 reborn in CXL memory expansion boxes
idea: Box: reclaimed DDR4 DIMMs x standard x standard x CXL controller with per-rank ECC remap and aging-aware refresh x refurbished chassis x refurbishment line. DDR4 from decommissioned servers is tested, graded and re-hosted behind CXL controllers that hide its latency for tier-2 data.
why: Supply: capacity with zero new wafers; tens of PB of DDR4 retire each year; cost per GB ~20-30% of new DDR5.

title: CNT vias failed on growth heat; transfer-grow iron-catalyzed CNT TSVs instead
idea: Carbon-nanotube vias (Fujitsu, imec) never reached production because good CNTs need ~700 C growth, incompatible with BEOL, and tip contact resistance was high. Grow dense vertical CNT forests from an Fe/Al2O3 catalyst (no Co) on a sacrificial carrier, transfer them into etched TSV holes with polymer fill, then Cu-plate the exposed tips, so the via is carbon in the barrel and Cu only at the contacts.
why: TSV CTE stress: CNT's near-zero CTE shrinks the transistor keep-out zone around each TSV ~3-5x, recovering die area lost to the HBM TSV tax (fact 6); no W or Co, ~100x Cu ampacity.

title: Sushi-conveyor optical delay-line ring for hot broadcast data
idea: Copy the kaiten-sushi conveyor. A closed, low-loss SiN waveguide loop on the interposer keeps tiny, very hot structures (MoE routing tables, norms, sync flags) circulating as WDM pulse trains. Each compute chiplet 'picks a plate' with a thermally tuned microring drop filter as the block goes by, and an on-loop re-timer re-injects the train every lap.
why: Serves many readers with no DRAM activation and no contention at the HBM PHY. Capacity is only kilobits per meter of loop, so the gain is modest: fewer hot-spot conflicts and roughly 5-10% fewer small HBM reads.

title: Downhole micro-Dewar layer lets DRAM sit directly atop hot GPUs
idea: Downhole logging tools survive 200 C by putting electronics in vacuum flasks. Insert a vacuum-gap/silica-aerogel interlayer between logic and a DRAM stack, crossed only by sparse hybrid-bonded copper pillars for signals, and give the DRAM its own top-side cold plate, so memory stays below 70 C while logic runs at 105 C.
why: Enables memory-on-logic 3D stacking (no interposer, mm-to-um wires, ~5-10x lower I/O energy) without the refresh doubling and retention loss that hit DRAM above 85 C.

title: Inductively coupled stack powered wirelessly: no TSV, no plating
idea: Box: DRAM x standard x on-die coil receivers x inductive data links plus resonant wireless power through 15 um dies x dry-plasma-thinned Si x laminated dry-film adhesive stack. Dies are glued with dry film, data crosses via coil pairs and power via a per-die resonant transformer, so TSV etch, Cu plating, CMP and their rinses disappear.
why: Water and TSV tax (fact 6): removes every wet TSV step, ~10-20x less water per stack, and recovers TSV keep-out area; power-transfer efficiency is the risk.

title: Inductively coupled tall stack wired only by two power bars
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Every tier talks to its neighbors through on-die coil pairs (no signal TSVs), and power enters through two thick copper bars plated into a single slot cut down the stack's side, so the only vertical metal in a 64-tier stack is power.
why: Removes signal TSVs and micro-bumps (fact 6) so interconnect cost no longer scales with tier count, enabling ~10x tiers per footprint at flat cost.

title: Beekeeper's honeycomb: hexagonal plasma-diced chiplets for more beachfront
idea: Bees tile with hexagons: plasma-dice compute and memory chiplets into hexagons so each compute die shares three or six full edges with memory dies in a honeycomb mesh, instead of a rectangle with only two usable sides.
why: Raises die-edge beachfront per mm2 by ~1.5-2x, so more memory channels attach per accelerator without TSV stacking: bandwidth per package goes up without HBM's area tax.

title: Glass micro-bridges with copper and laser-written waveguides
idea: MINIFY the interposer to small ~1x2 mm glass bridges placed only where die edges meet, each carrying fine copper lines plus femtosecond-laser-inscribed optical waveguides for longer hops.
why: Interposer cost and capital (CoWoS capacity): ~95% less silicon interposer area, with optics on the same bridge.

title: Prestressed-concrete trick: stress films flatten ultra-thin memory stacks
idea: Adapted from prestressed concrete: calibrated PECVD nitride/oxide films are deposited on the back of each thinned DRAM die so their built-in stress cancels the warpage that appears at bonding temperature. 30 um dies then stack flat with simple thermocompression.
why: Warpage limits HBM yield and stack height (fact 6); targets both using 1990s deposition tools.

title: Append-only KV log on NAND bonded beneath HBM
idea: Eliminate the flash translation layer and the SSD path for KV-cache spill: bond 3D NAND under the HBM base die and write KV caches as append-only logs aligned to erase blocks, erasing whole blocks when conversations expire, which matches NAND's native semantics so no mapping table, GC or write amplification is needed.
why: KV spill to SSD crosses PCIe at ~10-30 pJ/bit; in-stack NAND gives ~10x capacity per package at NAND cost/bit with only one fresh write per token.

title: Supermarket holographic scanners inspire free-space optical memory interconnect
idea: Adapted from the holographic optical elements in 1990s barcode scanners: a single cast hologram plate above the board redirects hundreds of VCSEL beams from memory packages to photodiodes on the processor, replacing board traces.
why: Board-level data movement and pin count: no copper trace loss, and routing is set by a cheap replicated hologram, so memory can be placed in 3D around the processor.

title: Optical clock trees failed on alignment; a light shaft through the stack
idea: Free-space optical clock distribution (1980s-2000s research) failed because external optics could not stay aligned to chips. Etch one 20-50 um oxide-lined vertical hole through every die of a memory stack so it acts as a light pipe, put an n-ZnO/p-NiO UV LED in the base die at its bottom, and let a ring photodiode on each die's shaft wall tap the pulse, broadcasting clock and command strobes to all tiers with sub-ps skew.
why: Removes clock/strobe TSVs and per-tier deskew circuits (fact 6), shrinking in-stack timing margins and power; uses only Zn, Ni, O and Si.

title: On-package antenna mesh replaces address and command wiring
idea: Substitute command/address wiring to every DRAM die with a ~300 GHz on-chip antenna broadcast network inside the package: the controller transmits each command once, all dies receive it simultaneously, and only data stays wired.
why: Facts 6/7: C/A pins and TSVs (~20-30% of HBM signals) disappear; more ranks per channel without electrical loading.

title: Jacquard-loom woven wire interposer for memory buses
idea: Adapted from programmable textile looms: 15-25 um insulated copper wires are woven into a fabric of crossing warp and weft. Insulation is laser-stripped at programmed crossings and welded to form a custom X-Y routing grid, which is embedded in epoxy as the processor-memory substrate.
why: Replaces lithographic interposers with loom automation plus a laser; capital-light and U.S.-manufacturable, with thick copper giving low-loss long buses.

title: Non-volatile PHY state enables nanosecond link sleep and wake
idea: Eliminate link retraining: store each lane's DFE taps, CTLE settings, phase offsets and VREF in ferroelectric latches inside the PHY, so the entire memory PHY can be power-gated between bursts and resume in <100 ns with no retraining.
why: PHYs burn ~20-30% of interface power idling to stay trained; gating between bursts cuts average IO energy ~30% on bursty inference traffic.

title: Transformer lamination stack with ferrite flux core through dies
idea: Treat thinned dies as transformer laminations: plug a ferrite flux-core post through the stack and wind thick-metal spiral coils on each 65 nm die around it. The core channels magnetic flux so all 16 tiers couple inductively without TSVs.
why: TSV-free wireless stacking made in mature nodes; removes TSV area tax and microbump yield loss.

title: Quorum-sensing analog bus for collective link width scaling
idea: Every memory chiplet leaks a current proportional to its queued demand onto one shared analog 'autoinducer' wire. The summed voltage acts like a bacterial quorum concentration: when it crosses thresholds, all PHYs together wake extra lanes or drop to narrow mode within nanoseconds, with no packet-based negotiation.
why: Idle I/O power: memory PHYs burn much of their power at low utilization; collective, instant width scaling could cut PHY idle energy 40-60%.

title: Memory cartridges: ship non-volatile modules instead of moving bytes
idea: Eliminate the network for bulk model distribution: package NV HBM-class stacks on hot-pluggable carriers written once at a central site and physically installed into inference servers, which execute directly from them as working memory.
why: A courier of 1 TB cartridges beats replicating a model to 10k servers over the network; removes petabytes of rollout traffic and boot-time weight loading.

title: Zn: ZnO piezo transducers send data acoustically through silicon stacks
idea: Sputter ZnO thin-film bulk-acoustic-wave transducers on every die so 1-5 GHz acoustic pulses carry data vertically through the bonded silicon stack (low acoustic loss in crystalline Si), with frequency-division channels per transducer; dies need a bonded acoustic path, not drilled and filled holes.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): hole-free stacking removes TSV keep-out zones and TSV yield loss; speculative ~0.5-1 pJ/bit links at modest per-channel rates.

title: Charge-recycling stacked I/O drivers
idea: MINIFY I/O energy by stacking four driver domains in series between VDD and ground, so the charge spent toggling one lane's wire flows on to drive the next, with level-shifted receivers.
why: Interface energy per bit: ideal ~4x lower supply current for the I/O; claims ~2.5x in practice.

title: Hydrogen tracer replaces helium for hermetic optics leak tests
idea: Substitute helium mass-spectrometer leak testing of hermetic optical-interconnect and memory packages with 5% hydrogen-in-nitrogen forming gas and low-cost MEMS palladium hydrogen sensors in a sniffer chamber.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% offline): keeps optical memory interconnect packaging running on a non-scarce gas; tester <$20k.

title: Display-driver tape-automated bonding puts memory dies on reel-to-reel film
idea: Adapted from the chip-on-film/TAB lines that bonded 1990s LCD driver chips: DRAM dies are bonded with anisotropic conductive film onto polyimide tape patterned at 20-30 um pitch, reel-to-reel and solder-free at 150-200 C. The memory tapes then attach around the processor.
why: Avoids micro-bump and hybrid-bonding tool chokepoints; reel-to-reel throughput and cheap film carriers give wide modest-pitch buses at low capital.

title: Cathedral builder's flying buttress: corner anchors carrying CTE strain
idea: Flying buttresses carry a wall's thrust outside it: place sintered-silver anchor pillars at the corners and edges of each memory die to take all shear from CTE mismatch, so the fine-pitch signal bonds in the field never see cyclic strain.
why: Fine-pitch signal joints survive 10 years of thermal cycling at 125 C, which allows denser, smaller bonds and so more bandwidth per mm of die edge.

title: Copper-sinter pastes failed from oxidation; formate copper replaces indium TIM
idea: Copper nanoparticle sinter pastes lost to silver sinter because Cu oxidized and needed hydrogen furnaces. Use Cu-formate complex inks that decompose in situ at ~200 C into fresh, oxide-free Cu, sintering a 20-50 um porous Cu layer between HBM/accelerator dies and the lid in place of indium solder and gallium liquid-metal thermal interfaces.
why: Removes In and Ga from the TIM of >700 W accelerator packages; sintered Cu (~100-200 W/m-K vs ~80 for In) keeps memory stacks cooler for more bandwidth and less refresh.

title: Nanoimprinted oxide-TFT memory built into glass package substrates
idea: Display fabs process glass at ~$100-300/m^2 versus ~$70,000/m^2 for finished DRAM wafers, a ~300x area-cost gap. Use nanoimprint lithography at 40-50 nm half-pitch on Gen-8 panels to pattern oxide-TFT gain cells, then cut the panel into glass-core package substrates carrying the memory directly under the chiplets.
why: At ~1/3 DRAM density, cost per bit ~100x lower and U.S.-manufacturable in display/glass lines; trades speed, retention and density.

title: Fiber-to-the-home splitter broadcasts model weights to many accelerators
idea: Adapted from passive optical networks (PON): a shared weight-memory pool transmits each layer's weights once on an optical channel, and a passive 1:32 splitter delivers the same stream to 32 accelerators at the same moment. Each accelerator keeps only KV-cache and activations in local HBM, not its own copy of the weights.
why: Replicated weights across data/pipeline-parallel GPUs waste scarce HBM; broadcast removes up to Nx duplication (30-60% of HBM freed per GPU) and replaces N reads with one.

title: Little's-law deep-queue byte interface over cheap NAND
idea: Bandwidth = bytes in flight / latency, so a 20 us medium delivers 1 TB/s if 20 MB are in flight. A controller chiplet beside the GPU exposes load/store addresses over SLC NAND with a 64k-entry tagged queue and 64 B read reassembly, while GPU warps hide the latency and an SRAM log absorbs writes.
why: Working memory at NAND cost (~100-200x cheaper per GB than 2026 DRAM); trades latency and write endurance.

title: Microfluidic interposer channels hold DRAM cool to cut refresh
idea: Worsen: put the hottest logic directly under DRAM so retention collapses and refresh doubles every ~10 C. Flip: etch microfluidic coolant channels in the interposer and base die between logic and memory so DRAM runs at ~45 C instead of ~90 C, stretching refresh intervals 4-8x.
why: Refresh (fact 3): refresh overhead falls from 10-20% to ~2-4% of bandwidth and idle power drops; also unblocks memory-on-logic stacking.

title: PCB-shop panel packaging with one stepper mask for die field
idea: Po: the memory package is made in a print shop. Large panels are patterned by maskless laser direct imaging for all coarse layers, and only the fine-pitch die-attach field uses one stepper mask, so U.S. PCB fabs can build HBM-class packages.
why: Onshore packaging capacity at lower capital per unit, easing the U.S. manufacturability gap.

title: Compact-disc scratch codes make TSV defects harmless
idea: Adapted from CD CIRC interleaving: each data word is spread across many TSVs with a Reed-Solomon erasure code, so a few open or leaky TSVs become erasures corrected on the fly instead of needing spare-TSV repair or scrapping the stack.
why: HBM yield down 20-30% (fact 6): could recover most TSV-related yield loss with ~10% extra wires and 180 nm codec logic.

title: Chip-on-glass display bonding builds memory cassettes for pennies
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Bond bare DRAM dies face-down onto 0.3 mm glass sheets with anisotropic conductive film exactly as LCD driver ICs are bonded (cents per bond, 1e5 bonds/day per line), then stack 20 sheets into a cassette with a flex edge connector.
why: Package substrate and socket cost (~$0.5-1 per die) disappears; sheets stack at ~0.4 mm pitch vs ~10 mm DIMM pitch, ~10x+ bits per volume at equal $/GB.

title: Rack daemon lends idle server RAM over RDMA
idea: Substitute buying more local DRAM with a kernel swap backend that pages cold memory into idle RAM on neighbouring servers via RDMA verbs, with replicated pages and fast failover.
why: Stranded memory (~20-30%): fleets buy ~15% fewer DIMMs; pure software from a small team.

title: Beforehand cushioning: reusable sacrificial test tier for known-good stacks
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: after each bonding step, attach a reusable probe die with dense test circuits to the top of the partial stack, using micro-spring contacts and a low-temperature debondable adhesive. It tests every tier and TSV so bad partial stacks are reworked or dropped before more good dies go on, then it is lifted off and reused.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): good dies are no longer stacked onto bad partial stacks, so stack yield rises from ~70% to ~90% and effective HBM cost per GB falls ~20%.

title: Excessive action: 65,536-bit ultra-wide, ultra-slow hybrid-bonded bus
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial or excessive action: make the bus 32x wider than HBM3 using 3 um hybrid-bond pitch, but run each pin at only 200-400 Mb/s with unterminated 0.4 V inverter drivers and no SerDes, DLL or training.
why: Data movement (fact 5): ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit IO at HBM3E-class bandwidth, and the PHY shrinks because its circuits are trivial.

title: Clockless delay-insensitive memory channel without DLLs or training
idea: Eliminate the clock: replace DDR strobes, DLLs, PLLs and link training on short on-package links with a 1-of-4 delay-insensitive code (2 bits on 4 wires, one transition per symbol, receiver detects completion and acknowledges). Timing adapts automatically to voltage, temperature and process.
why: Clocking and training are ~20-30% of PHY power/area and idle clocks burn energy; a self-timed link targets ~0.3 pJ/bit with zero idle power and permits aggressive voltage scaling below today's IO floor.

title: Qi wireless-charging coils powering each stacked die
idea: Phones charge on a pad. Pattern thin planar Cu coils in each die's back-end RDL (≤250 C) and a driver coil in the base die, so power crosses the stack inductively at tens of MHz. Signals cross on capacitive coupling pads.
why: Removes power TSVs, about half of all TSVs, easing HBM's TSV tax and yield loss. Feasibility depends on reaching ~70% link efficiency.

title: Piezo: GHz ultrasonic through-silicon acoustic vias replace HBM data TSVs
idea: Pattern thin-film ScAlN bulk-acoustic transducers on each thinned DRAM die; data rides as 5-10 GHz longitudinal ultrasound pulses straight through the bonded silicon stack, each die's transducer tuned to its own frequency band so one acoustic column serves 16 dies. No holes are drilled, so TSV keep-out zones and TSV-induced yield loss disappear.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): recovers TSV+KOZ area (~5-10% of die) and part of the 20-30% stack yield loss; per-column bandwidth ~10-20 Gb/s, so best for command/address, ECC and sideband lanes first.

title: Traversal descriptors replace command-address pins entirely
idea: Scarcity: zero command/address pins. The host writes a compact traversal program (base, strides, gather-index pointer, tile shape) into a sequencer in the memory base die once; memory then streams data in consumption order with only a 1-bit flow-control backchannel.
why: Frees ~25-30% of interface pins for data and removes CA energy; the sequencer sees the whole access pattern and orders activations to cut fact-8 page overfetch 2-4x on tensor workloads.

title: Chandelier: DRAM blades hung edge-on perpendicular to processor
idea: Forced 'chandelier': DRAM dies are mounted vertically, edge-on, like hanging crystals, with sidewall pads soldered to the processor substrate. Coolant flows between the blades, and 32 or more blades fit per package with no TSVs.
why: TSV tax and stack thermal limits; vertical orientation gives every die its own short edge link and its own cooling surface.

title: Vinyl-record hot-embossed polymer optical couplers for memory links
idea: Hot-emboss V-grooves, waveguides and 45-degree mirrors into cyclic-olefin polymer in seconds, as vinyl records and DVDs are replicated from a nickel master. Fiber arrays then align passively to memory photonic dies.
why: Optical coupler cost and alignment time drop ~10x, making optical memory links affordable at volume.

title: Adaptive patterning wires each module to measured die positions
idea: Invert 'wiring masks are fixed before chips are placed': place DRAM and logic dies loosely, measure each die's true position and write custom redistribution per package with maskless lithography (Arizona adaptive-patterning lines).
why: Cheap placement plus maskless wiring gives fine-pitch memory links without CoWoS-class bonders or masks; lower capital per unit and an all-U.S. flow.

title: Microfabricated ferrite-core planes plated onto package substrates
idea: Worsen: make memory require the most advanced lithography. Flip: plate few-micron NiZn-ferrite or permalloy micro-toroids on organic or glass substrate panels, threaded by lithographic X/Y/sense lines, reviving core memory with PCB-class tools: no capacitor, no transistor per bit, unlimited endurance.
why: Scarce-resource and U.S. manufacturability: panel processes, no EUV; low density (~50 MB per layer per 100 cm^2) suits persistent buffers and tables.

title: LED-strip memory tape spools gigabytes into empty chassis space
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Mount DRAM dies every 5 mm along a flat polyimide ribbon with a shared differential serial bus, built on reel-to-reel LED-strip SMT lines, and coil or fold the tape into chassis voids alongside cooling ducts.
why: Uses volume DIMM slots cannot reach at LED-strip assembly cost (fractions of a cent per placement): ~10x bits per chassis liter vs DIMMs.

title: Copper nanowire velcro: room-temperature interlocking die bonds
idea: Substitute solder microbumps and thermocompression with electroplated copper nanowire forests grown through porous-alumina templates on both mating pads; pressed together at room temperature they interlock and cold-weld at 5 um pitch.
why: Fact 6 and Fact 3: no thermal budget hit to DRAM retention, a simple press replaces a ~$2M TCB tool, bond yield improves.

title: Mercury delay line reborn: fiber-loop memory circulating AI weights at light speed
idea: Delay-line memory died because data was only available as it came round (sequential access) and the medium drifted with temperature. LLM inference reads every weight in the same order each token, so sequential access is fine: a ~10 km multicore-fiber loop (19 cores x C+L WDM, ~1 Pb/s) holds several GB in flight with all-optical amplifiers and a clock-recovering regenerator every few laps, and taps feed each accelerator as its layer's weights come round.
why: HBM capacity and data movement (facts 5, 6): weights delivered at ~100 TB/s with holding cost set by amplifier power (tens of W) rather than DRAM bits, freeing HBM for KV cache; claimed 2-5x less HBM for weight-streaming inference.

title: Open replaceable memory chiplet standard tied to procurement
idea: MAGNIFY interchangeability: an open mechanical and electrical spec for socketed memory chiplets (UCIe-style), required in federally funded AI clusters, so any vendor's memory can be swapped.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply resilience: new domestic memory makers can sell into installed systems; repair beats scrap.

title: Stained-glass mosaic interposer from known-good DUV tiles
idea: Make small reticle-size interposer tiles on DUV lines, test them, and join them like stained glass with printed bridge seams playing the lead came, building panels of more than four reticles.
why: Breaks the reticle limit for memory-rich packages without EUV or risky stitching; known-good tiles lift yield.

title: Prior action: weights stored entropy-coded, decoded by 28 nm ingress engines
idea: TRIZ #10 Preliminary action: compress model weights offline with per-tensor entropy coding (Huffman/ANS on quantized values) and keep them compressed in DRAM. A 28 nm decoder chiplet at the accelerator's memory ingress expands them at line rate. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capacity and data movement (fact 5): 1.4-2x fewer DRAM bits and link bits per weight, with the decode logic built in trailing fabs.

title: Voltage-stacked HBM recycling one current through every die
idea: Po: every die stands on a different ground. Wire the 8-16 dies' supplies in series (die k between kV and (k+1)V), feed the stack at ~12 V, and use small on-die switched-capacitor balancers plus level-shifted signalling so the same current flows through all dies.
why: Supply current and power TSV/bump count drop 8-16x; since power and ground are a large share of TSVs, stack area and PDN loss fall sharply.

title: VO2 Mott hysteresis gives a one-element volatile latch
idea: Worsen: require a capacitor to remember a bit. Flip: bias a nanoscale VO2 element inside its insulator-metal hysteresis window, where it stays either metallic or insulating; a short pulse flips it and a small read current senses resistance, giving a one-resistor-one-selector latch stacked in the link die BEOL.
why: Near cross-point density, refresh-free while biased, nanosecond switching and high reported endurance; holding current is the energy risk.

title: Tide: lanes reverse direction as read/write traffic ebbs and flows
idea: Like tides: memory link lanes are bidirectional and are reassigned between read and write direction every microsecond from traffic counters, so read-heavy inference gets nearly all the lanes.
why: Bandwidth per wire, about 1.6x effective read bandwidth for inference, so fewer pins, TSVs or stacks are needed.

title: Bit-plane sliced stacks make data movement proportional to precision
idea: Scarcity: no reading bits the model will not use. Each die in a 16-high stack holds one bit-plane (die 0 = sign/MSB) and the base die reassembles words, so an FP4 inference read activates only the top 4 dies while FP16 training reads all 16.
why: Data movement and activation energy (facts 5, 8): low-precision reads cost ~4x less energy and bandwidth with no reformatting of stored weights.

title: Sushi conveyor: time-slotted page carousel ring for shared reads
idea: Memory chiplets put pages onto a circulating, time-slotted ring bus like dishes on a sushi belt; every accelerator snoops the passing slot and takes what it needs. Shared data such as batched-inference weights is read from DRAM once and consumed by N devices.
why: Data-movement energy and bandwidth for broadcast data: N-fold fewer DRAM reads of shared weights, so fewer HBM stacks are needed per cluster.

title: Military fuzz-button connectors make solderless, reworkable memory stacks
idea: Adapted from fuzz-button (compressed gold-wire wad) interconnects in avionics: DRAM dies or packages stack in a clamped frame with fuzz-button arrays between them, so any failing die can be swapped after test with no reflow.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): one bad die no longer scraps a 12-16 die stack (~20-30% yield recovery), using 1990s machining and wire-forming tools.

title: Factory-seconds HBM: sell partly failed stacks as shorter SKUs
idea: Like outlet garments, stacks with one or two dead dies get fused-off remap in the base die and ship as 8- or 10-high parts instead of being scrapped. Pricing tiers make the seconds a market.
why: Recovers a large share of the 20-30% stacking yield loss as sellable bits, a fast supply gain with no new fab.

title: Volume-holographic weight crystals read by light into compute
idea: Ideal: weights held in a passive crystal and read by a flash of light. Closest achievable: record each layer's weight pages as angle-multiplexed holograms in a photopolymer or LiNbO3 block; a steered laser reconstructs one ~1 Mb page per pulse onto a photodiode array bonded to the accelerator, with no refresh and no electrical storage.
why: Zero refresh and page-parallel Tb/s reads of frozen weights at low pJ/bit; TB-per-cm3 class capacity offloads weights from DRAM entirely, though random access is microseconds, so it suits streaming.

title: Flash-resident KV cache with attention-guided prefetch over CXL
idea: Box: dense 3D NAND x standard x standard x CXL/optical link with predictive prefetch engine x SSD x standard. The LLM KV cache lives on flash; a small predictor in the controller uses top-k attention scores to prefetch the token blocks the next step needs into a 10x smaller DRAM buffer.
why: Water and DRAM demand: ~10x less DRAM per served session; NAND needs far less fab water per bit, so memory water per session falls ~10x.

title: Accumulate-on-write: the host sends sums, never reads back
idea: Reverse read-modify-write ownership: the interface gains an 'add' write command, and the HBM base die does the read, the BF16/FP32 add and the write-back next to the array, so gradient accumulation, optimizer moments and KV updates never cross the link twice.
why: Halves link traffic in accumulation-heavy training phases, ~30-50% of optimizer-step bytes (fact 5), and lets ECC be recomputed locally.

title: Abacus: accumulate-on-write memory-side atomics halve gradient traffic
idea: Like beads sliding on an abacus: the memory controller on an FPGA card adds incoming partial sums into stored values, so writes are atomic accumulate operations and no read-modify-write round trip is needed.
why: Halves link traffic for gradient accumulation and histograms; saves both energy and bandwidth.

title: Magnetically aligned nanowire underfill replacing microbumps
idea: Combine anisotropic conductive film with magnetic-field assembly: Ni-cored, Au-shelled nanowires dispersed in a curable underfill chain into vertical columns between pads under a field applied during bonding, then cure, giving 2-5 um pitch z-axis interconnect with no microbump plating or Cu CMP.
why: HBM stacking cost and warpage tolerance: claims 30-50% lower stacking cost and reworkable joints.

title: Vacuum-tube mica revival: muscovite sheets as PTFE-free high-speed dielectric
idea: Revive mica, the dielectric of early capacitors and tube spacers: cleave natural muscovite to 10-25 um sheets and laminate it with copper by adhesive-free thermocompression as the high-speed layers for memory-to-logic package traces.
why: Constraint: replaces PTFE-based laminates used for >50 GHz links; mica has tan-delta ~0.0002 and atomically flat surfaces for fine lines, and is mined in the U.S. (North Carolina) and India.

title: CDMA-coded shared vertical bus: eight dies talk on one wire
idea: Scarcity: only one-eighth of the normal TSV count is allowed. Each die spreads its data with an orthogonal Walsh code onto shared vertical wires, and the base die correlates to separate the simultaneous transmissions, trading symbol rate for wire count.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): 4-8x fewer TSVs cut keep-out area and TSV yield loss while keeping aggregate stack bandwidth.

title: SrTiO3 DRAM capacitors failed on leakage; decaps tolerate it
idea: Strontium titanate (k ~100-300) was abandoned for DRAM storage capacitors because its leakage was far too high for fA-level retention and it wanted Ru electrodes. Power decoupling tolerates ~1000x more leakage, so deposit STO on TiN electrodes in deep trenches of the interposer or base die for several-uF/mm2 decaps that steady ultra-wide I/O supplies, replacing Ta capacitors and Hf/Zr-oxide MIMs.
why: Lets HBM-class I/O run at lower VDDQ with thinner noise margins (facts 5, 10) and removes Ta, Hf and Ru from memory power delivery; Sr, Ti, O and N only.

title: Voltage-stacked DRAM tiers slash power bumps by four
idea: Scarcity: only 15% of bumps may carry power. Put 4 DRAM dies in series voltage domains (each floating 1.1 V above the one below on a 4.4 V rail) so one current flows through all tiers; small switched-capacitor balancers absorb mismatch and signals cross domains through capacitive level shifters.
why: Power uses over half of stack bumps/TSVs; series stacking cuts supply current 4x, freeing bumps for data and cutting IR drop, ~1.5x bandwidth per stack footprint.

title: Fluidic self-assembly of shape-keyed memory tiles
idea: Reverse pick-and-place: diced memory tiles with keyed asymmetric outlines tumble in a fluid over a logic wafer etched with matching recesses, and the capillary pull of molten low-temperature solder in each recess drags tiles into ~1 um alignment, assembling thousands in parallel.
why: Capital intensity of placement and bonding tools; parallel assembly makes many small, high-yield memory tiles economical.

title: Fluidic self-assembly drops DRAM dies into hybrid-bond sites
idea: Scarcity: die bonders are the bottleneck tool. Dies with a keyed outline and hydrophobic backside are tumbled in a carrier liquid over a logic wafer with matching hydrophilic recesses; capillary forces self-align them to <0.5 um and the wafer is batch-annealed into Cu-Cu hybrid bonds.
why: Packaging capital intensity: replaces ~1,000 dies/hr pick-and-place with wafer-parallel placement (1e4-1e5 dies/hr per tank), ~10x less bonding capex per stack.

title: Cordwood-module revival: edge-standing DRAM dies plug into logic like books
idea: Revive Apollo-era cordwood construction: thinned DRAM dies with I/O routed to one edge stand perpendicular to the logic die like books on a shelf, their laser-diced edge pads finished with PFAS-free electroless Ni/Au and joined to a grid of landing pads.
why: Constraint: no TSV etch or fluorinated plating additives; each die gets its own full-edge I/O (10 mm x 25 pads/mm = 250+ signals) instead of sharing through-stack vias, and coolant can flow between the 'books'.

title: Z-channel coding exploits one-way charge leakage at the interface encoder
idea: Use the physics timescale of leakage: retention errors almost only turn stored charge to no-charge, so the interface encoder maps data to true/anti-cell polarity to minimize charged cells and applies an asymmetric (Z-channel) code. At 1% one-directional error, capacity rises from 0.92 to ~0.95 and parity needs fall ~40%.
why: Cuts ECC overhead for 1%-BER cells and reduces charged-cell count (refresh and CV2 energy, facts 3, 10) by ~20-30%.

title: ESD-free die-to-die pads via laser-cut sacrificial shorting ring
idea: ESD diodes often contribute over half of an I/O pad's capacitance, yet they only matter during handling. Tie all bond pads to a metal shorting ring through dicing and stacking, then laser-ablate or fuse the ring after bonding, leaving bare pads at ~1-2 fF instead of ~100 fF.
why: 2-4x lower CV^2 per bit on chiplet and HBM links and smaller I/O area (facts 5, 7).

title: Water-slide decal transfer of thin DRAM layers by laser lift-off
idea: Like water-slide decals, build DRAM layers on a sacrificial release film and bond them to a logic wafer with ≤250 C adhesive or hybrid bonding. Laser lift-off then frees the carrier, avoiding Smart Cut's ~500 C split anneal. Repeat for multiple layers.
why: Layers 2-5 um thick allow ~1 um via pitch, versus ~40 um for TSVs: ~100x denser vertical interconnect and far lower pJ/bit than HBM.

title: ESD-free hybrid-bond IO for wafer-level-only stacks
idea: Eliminate ESD protection on internal die-to-die pads: hybrid-bonded faces are never touched by humans or probes after bonding, so drop ESD diodes and use a sacrificial wafer-level discharge grid that is severed during bonding, shrinking pad capacitance from ~200 fF to ~10 fF.
why: IO energy is CV^2 dominated by pad capacitance: vertical-link energy/bit falls ~5-10x and smaller pads allow 2-3x more vertical channels in the same area.

title: Sidewall-written stack wiring replaces TSVs in DRAM cubes
idea: Substitute TSVs with wiring on the stack's faces: dies route pads to their edges, the stacked cube's sides are planarized, then copper traces are laser-direct-written down each sidewall; four faces give ~4,000 lines per cube at 10 um pitch.
why: Fact 6: removes TSV area tax and the TSV process module (~30% of HBM packaging cost), allowing near-standard dies to be stacked.

title: FPGA retimer that compresses cache lines in flight
idea: Substitute raw transfers on a CXL memory link with an inline FPGA stage doing base-delta-immediate plus zero-run coding of 64 B lines, packing 2-3 compressed lines into each flit in both directions.
why: Fact 5: effective link bandwidth +1.5-2x and expander capacity +1.3-1.8x for typical data, delivered as pure logic design.

title: Base-die line compressor storing size tags in spare ECC bits
idea: Combine the HBM base die with a hardware cache-line compressor (base-delta plus shared FP8/BF16 exponents) whose per-line size tag lives in spare ECC/metadata bits, so two compressed lines pack into one slot transparently and the host sees normal addresses.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: 1.3-2x effective capacity and bandwidth on AI tensors with no host software change.

title: Decal transfer printing of lasers onto mature-node base die
idea: Use an elastomer stamp, like a water-slide decal, to pick thousands of InP lasers and photodiodes per stroke from their native wafer and print them onto a 28-65 nm HBM base die. The memory stack then gets optical I/O.
why: Optical memory I/O at ~1 pJ/bit with no advanced node; distance-free links decouple memory from compute shoreline.

title: Contactless inductive wafer probing at full speed for known-good dies
idea: Combine inductive-coupling transceivers with wafer sort: every DRAM core die carries a small coil-array test port so the prober couples wirelessly at full 6-10 Gb/s and runs retention, row-hammer and speed screens before thinning and stacking, with no probe damage or large test pads.
why: HBM yield (down 20-30%): stacking only truly known-good dies could recover about half that loss and remove test-pad area.

title: Epoch-tagged dual-slot lines make crash consistency fence-free
idea: Eliminate persist barriers and write-ahead logging: each NV line has two slots; writes go to the uncommitted slot tagged with a hardware epoch, and a single per-epoch commit record flips which slot is valid, so recovery discards incomplete epochs automatically.
why: Logging doubles NV write traffic and fences stall pipelines; dual-slot epochs halve write bandwidth for persistent data structures and remove ordering stalls (~2x throughput).

title: DRAM die as the bridge between compute chiplets
idea: Invert 'bridges are just wires': embed a DRAM die as the EMIB-style bridge between two U.S.-fabbed logic dies (Intel Arizona/New Mexico packaging, U.S.-made DRAM), so the die carrying die-to-die wires also stores what they exchange.
why: Memory sits on the communication path; inter-chiplet buffers and KV need no HBM round trip, ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit and fewer HBM bits spent on staging.

title: Shingled face-to-face die tiles talk by capacitive overlap
idea: Scarcity: no interposer and no substrate wiring between dies. Lay DRAM and logic dies like roof shingles, alternating face-up and face-down so each edge overlaps its neighbor by 1 mm; 20 um capacitive pads in the overlap couple data across a thin oxide gap.
why: Interposer cost and TSV tax: no wires or TSVs, ~1-2 Tb/s per mm of overlap at <0.5 pJ/bit near-field coupling; packaging becomes mechanical placement.

title: Depreciated non-EUV fabs feed forty-tier capacity stacks
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Source 1x/2x-nm-class DRAM dies from fully depreciated, EUV-free lines (wafer cost ~1/3 of leading edge since depreciation is ~55% of cost) and stack 40 tiers per footprint so tiers, not lithography, deliver bits per mm2 of board.
why: Capital intensity and litho-bound scaling (fact 4): a node buys only 10-20% cost per bit, while 40 cheap tiers buy ~10x density per footprint at the same $/GB.

title: Harvested server DIMMs reborn as U.S.-assembled CXL memory pools
idea: Invert 'memory supply must be freshly fabricated': collect DDR4/DDR5 from retired U.S. hyperscaler servers, test and bin in U.S. plants, and remount on CXL expander cards with a domestic controller as a warm tier behind HBM.
why: Millions of GB retire yearly; reuse adds usable supply at near-zero wafer cost while new DRAM is 4x pricier, at ~$1-2/GB refurbishment cost.

title: Bookshelf memory: dies stand on edge in a silicon comb
idea: Invert 'dies stack flat on top of each other': thin DRAM dies are inserted vertically like books into a deep-etched silicon comb, I/O routed to one edge and joined by sidewall metallization to the comb floor; each die's full edge is its beachfront and heat flows in-plane to a top cold plate.
why: No TSVs, no 30 um thinning, no vertical thermal stacking penalty; aims at HBM-class density and bandwidth at near-DDR5 wafer area per bit (removing much of the ~3x HBM area tax).

title: N: silicon-nitride linear-drive optics extend DDR5 slots off-board
idea: Insert a linear, non-retimed optical extender at each DDR5 socket: Si3N4/SiP modulators driven directly by the DQ/DQS analog waveforms and photodiodes at a remote liquid-cooled DIMM tray 0.3-1 m away, with the host's existing read/write leveling absorbing the extra ~3-5 ns flight time.
why: Capacity per socket and data movement with interface unchanged: DIMMs leave the crowded board, allowing 2-4x more DIMMs per CPU and better cooling, at ~2-4 pJ/bit added.

title: Wartime auto-plant conversion: idle U.S. 200 mm fabs make interposers
idea: Adapted from Willow Run's conversion from cars to bombers: shuttered or underused U.S. 200 mm/180 nm fabs are retooled to make passive silicon interposers, RDL and DRIE TSVs, all of which need only 0.5-2 um features.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: packaging capacity in months at ~10% of new-fab cost, easing the CoWoS-class bottleneck that gates HBM.

title: Clockless delay-insensitive DRAM interface eliminating DLLs and PLLs
idea: Abandon the global nanosecond clock: data moves with dual-rail or level-encoded handshakes so each transfer completes when it completes, and the DRAM drops its DLL, which burns power even when idle. Bus speed tracks voltage and temperature automatically.
why: Removes DLL/PLL standby power and worst-case timing guard bands: ~20-30% lower interface energy at low utilization.

title: Continuity of useful action: full-duplex simultaneous bidirectional TSVs
idea: TRIZ #20 Continuity of useful action: add hybrid echo-cancelling receivers to every DQ TSV so reads and writes flow on the same wire at the same time. This removes read-write turnaround bubbles and the idle direction.
why: Data movement and HBM TSV tax (facts 5, 6): recovers the 10-20% lost to turnaround and gives up to 2x bandwidth per TSV, so half the DQ TSVs deliver the same bandwidth.

title: Ethernet hybrid echo cancellation for simultaneous bidirectional TSVs
idea: Gigabit Ethernet runs both directions on one pair with a hybrid and an echo canceller. Do the same in HBM: each TSV/microbump carries read and write data at once, and a replica-driver hybrid subtracts the die's own transmitted signal.
why: Doubles bandwidth per TSV or bump, or halves the data-TSV count at the same bandwidth. Either way it directly cuts HBM's ~3x area-per-bit TSV tax.

title: Plumber's two-way pipe: simultaneous bidirectional interposer wires
idea: A plumber's pipe carries flow both ways in a heat exchanger: drive each HBM data wire from both ends at once and cancel your own transmitted signal with a hybrid echo canceller at each receiver, so every wire carries read and write traffic at the same time.
why: Halves the bumps and interposer wires per unit of bandwidth (or doubles bandwidth), which eases the beachfront limit and interposer cost; ~0.4 pJ/bit.

title: Bookshelf packaging stands DRAM dies on edge at 60 um pitch
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Route all die I/O to one edge, wafer-level plate that edge into contact fingers, and slot dies vertically like books into a glass rack whose floor carries the bus; no TSVs or stacking bonders, and coolant flows between the books.
why: Footprint density: a 10 x 10 mm rack holds ~150 standing dies vs 1 flat die, and edge plating is cheaper per die than TSV stacking.

title: Liquid-metal micro-wells make chiplet memory reworkable
idea: Substitute solder joints with laser-etched micro-wells in the substrate filled with gallium-indium alloy over a nickel barrier; die pillars plunge into the wells for contact, and a failed memory die lifts out cold and is replaced.
why: Yield and cost: rework instead of scrapping multi-die packages, run with dispensing and lamination equipment a small team owns.

title: Dry-grown carbon nanotube forests as compliant memory interconnects
idea: Box: DRAM x standard x standard x CNT-forest bumps densified and metal-capped x Si x dry thermal CVD growth plus ALD metal cap. Compliant CNT pillars absorb +/-1 um topography, so dies stack without CMP flattening, plating or solder flux.
why: Water: removes CMP, plating and flux wash (>10x); compliance tolerates thin-die warpage; contact resistance is the risk.

title: Spark-gap revival: impulse radio broadcasts between chiplets inside package cavity
idea: Revive spark-gap carrierless transmission as on-chip impulse UWB: memory chiplets radiate 20-50 ps pulses from on-die antennas into the metal-lid cavity, and compute chiplets receive with crystal-set-style envelope detectors (no PLL or LO).
why: Constraint: wireless links need no TSVs, no fluorinated etch and no PTFE high-frequency substrate; broadcast fan-out of weights is free at ~1-3 pJ/bit and 10-20 Gb/s per channel.

title: CCD memory reborn as charge-packet data bus inside DRAM periphery
idea: 1970s CCD memories lost to DRAM because serial shifting made random access slow, yet moving charge packets down a buried channel is extremely cheap per hop. Use a short CCD-style bucket-brigade channel to carry the 128-256 bits fetched from a bank toward the I/O hub as charge packets clocked at ~0.3 V, instead of full-swing global I/O lines, serializing the data naturally as it moves.
why: On-die data movement (facts 5, 8): global I/O wiring is a large share of DRAM read energy; claimed 2-4x lower on-die transport energy per bit and fewer long metal lines in the periphery (fact 7).

title: Octopus nerve ring: stack-to-stack shortcut bypassing the processor
idea: Octopus arms exchange signals through a nerve ring without involving the brain. In the same way, the HBM base dies around an accelerator get a ring of short interposer links to their neighbours, so KV-cache moves, page migration and memory-side reductions go stack-to-stack without crossing the GPU's PHYs and on-chip network.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): removes two PHY crossings and a NoC hop for memory-to-memory traffic, ~2x less energy for those transfers and more host bandwidth for compute.

title: Spike-timing code: one edge carries several bits by position
idea: Instead of NRZ or PAM4 levels, each symbol window carries a single transition placed in one of 8-16 time slots (pulse-position coding, like neurons encoding information in spike timing), so each transition carries 3-4 bits. Transition count, the main CV^2 cost of a wire, falls.
why: Link energy (facts 5 and 10): ~3x fewer transitions per bit at the same swing; on capacitive interposer wires that is roughly a 2-3x pJ/bit cut, paid for with finer timing.
